| Coverage | Consensus error (if random) | Implied $Q$ |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | $1.3\times10^{-4}$ | 39 |

| 30 | $7.7\times10^{-21}$ | 201 |

These numbers are absurd, and that is the point: real nanopore consensus does not reach $Q200$. The model fails because its central assumption is wrong. At a homopolymer, the errors are not independent; every read makes the same miscall, so the error survives averaging no matter how deep the coverage. review_corrections.new:
**3. Why coverage does not rescue a systematic error.** Suppose the single-read error probability is $p=0.05$ and observations are independent. If $K$ is the number of erroneous observations among $n$ reads, then $K$ is binomial. More than half the observations being correct guarantees a correct majority call, so a conservative error bound is
$$P_{\mathrm{error}}\leq\sum_{k=\lceil n/2\rceil}^{n}\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}.$$
For even $n$, ties are conservatively included as failures. This bound groups all wrong bases together; it is not an exact four-base consensus error model.

| Coverage | Error upper bound (independent model) | Corresponding $Q$ lower bound |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | $0.0012$ | 29 |
| 10 | $6.4e-05$ | 42 |
| 30 | $2.3e-12$ | 116 |

Even these conservative model estimates become unrealistically small. Real nanopore errors include correlated sequence-context effects, particularly at homopolymers; their probability does not shrink according to an independent binomial model. More coverage helps random error, but correlated errors require improved chemistry and base calling. These figures illustrate the statistical assumption rather than predicting real instrument accuracy.

review_corrections.old: **An industrial example: removing proteins in sugar processing.** Sugar beets are washed, ground and filtered to leave a feed rich in sugar and various proteins. The aim is to precipitate the proteins and keep the sugar. A **gradient of pH** is established along a horizontal tank with stirrers, so that **in each compartment a different protein reaches its own pI and precipitates**. A protein-free sugar solution is finally produced. The process is used at the British Sugar plant in Bury St Edmunds.
review_corrections.new: **Conceptual example: staged pH-controlled precipitation.** If a mixture contains proteins with different solubility minima, successive compartments can adjust pH and remove precipitated fractions. Actual recovery also depends on residence time, mixing and overlapping solubility curves. Commercial beet-juice clarification uses lime treatment and removal of impurities; the schematic should not be taken as evidence that a particular sugar factory fractionates proteins one by one at their pI.
review_corrections.reason: British Sugar describes lime clarification; remove unsupported specific factory/pI-fractionation claim.

review_corrections.old: This is the key idea made into equipment: because each protein has its own pI, a *spatial* pH gradient separates a mixture into fractions in one continuous unit.
review_corrections.new: The schematic illustrates how pH-dependent solubility can guide equipment design. It does not guarantee individual protein fractions: proteins can have overlapping precipitation ranges.
review_corrections.reason: Distinct pIs do not guarantee fractionation.

review_corrections.old: Because the binding site is conserved and distinct from the variable region (Section 27), one resin captures essentially *any* IgG regardless of what it binds.
review_corrections.new: Fc binding makes capture largely independent of antigen specificity, but affinity depends on species and IgG subclass; human IgG3 is a common weak/non-binding exception. The ligand and operating conditions must therefore be checked for the actual antibody.
review_corrections.reason: Protein A is not universal across IgG subclasses/species.

review_corrections.source: out/merged/Advanced Biotechnology 14 - Chromatography and final isolation.md
review_corrections.old: **Why five types rather than one.** Each exploits a different molecular property — polarity, partition, size, charge, specific binding — so impurities that resemble the product in one property usually differ in another. Real purification trains therefore run **several types in series**: for an antibody, typically Protein A affinity first (very high selectivity, low capacity), then ion exchange, then gel filtration as a polishing step.
review_corrections.new: **Why combine types.** Each exploits a different molecular property — polarity, partition, size, charge or specific binding — so impurities that resemble the product in one property may differ in another. Antibody purification commonly uses Protein A capture followed by one or more polishing steps such as ion exchange. Size exclusion can remove aggregates, especially at laboratory scale, but its loading and dilution limits mean it is not a universal final step in manufacturing.
review_corrections.reason: Avoid implying every industrial antibody train ends with SEC.

review_corrections.source: out/merged/Advanced Biotechnology 14 - Chromatography and final isolation.md
review_corrections.old: **The capacity/selectivity trade.** Affinity is the most selective and the most expensive: Protein A resin costs orders of magnitude more per litre than ion-exchange resin, and it degrades. Gel chromatography is cheap and gentle but has low capacity, because the sample volume must be small compared with the column. This is why affinity goes first, when the volume is largest and the impurity load greatest, and gel filtration last.
review_corrections.new: **The capacity/selectivity trade.** Affinity can provide strong selectivity at high resin cost. Capacity depends on ligand density, accessible pores and operating conditions; it is not necessarily low. High-resolution size exclusion has a small sample-volume limit, making it useful for polishing suitable partly purified samples. Resin cost and lifetime, loading, resolution and recovery must be compared for the actual process.
review_corrections.reason: Affinity capacity and resin cost are process-dependent; SEC not universally cheap.

review_corrections.source: out/merged/Advanced Biotechnology 14 - Chromatography and final isolation.md
review_corrections.old: **HPLC (high-performance liquid chromatography)** achieves better resolution, using **small particles (2 to 5 µm)** and **high pressure (5–10 MPa)**. Throughput is low, 1 to 5 mL min⁻¹. It is used at small scale or laboratory scale, and also for valuable products — oligonucleotide purification (Section 06) is the example already met.
review_corrections.new: **HPLC (high-performance liquid chromatography)** often uses fine particles and sufficiently high pressure to control band spreading. Analytical systems commonly use micrometre-scale particles and low flow rates, but pressure and throughput depend on the column and duty; preparative HPLC also exists. Oligonucleotide purification (Section 06) is one application.
review_corrections.reason: Instrument categories do not impose fixed resolution/flow/pressure ranges.

review_corrections.source: out/merged/Advanced Biotechnology 14 - Chromatography and final isolation.md
review_corrections.old: **FPLC (fast protein liquid chromatography)** has lower resolution, **larger particles**, lower pressure and higher throughput, and is used at larger scale.
review_corrections.new: **FPLC (fast protein liquid chromatography)** describes systems designed for protein purification with compatible wetted materials, aqueous buffers, gradient control and fraction collection. They are used from laboratory purification to process development. Resolution depends on the resin, column and operating conditions, rather than being intrinsically lower than HPLC; pressure and flow limits depend on the particular system and column.
review_corrections.reason: FPLC is not intrinsically low resolution or exclusively large-scale.
